paper_title: MTEdit: Packed Trajectories Beat Rollouts for Multi-Turn Image Editing

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, making it better aligned with human-AI collaborative creation than single-turn editing. However, constructing high-quality multi-turn training data remains challenging, as conventional sequential rollout accumulates errors and introduces visual-quality drift across editing turns. To address this challenge, we introduce MTEdit, a multi-turn image editing dataset built through a pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. By jointly generating multiple editing states within a unified visual context, this pipeline reduces visual-quality drift across turns. Covering both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios, MTEdit comprises 500K multi-turn image editing trajectories, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, making it one of the most extensive datasets for multi-turn image editing. We further introduce MTEdit-Bench, a benchmark designed to evaluate both scenarios by assessing models' ability to follow editing instructions, maintain content consistency, resist visual-quality drift, and effectively use historical context across turns. Using MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. On MTEdit-Bench, we evaluate a broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Experimental results show that Qwen-Image-MTEdit achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving models' multi-turn image editing capabilities.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Recently, multi-turn image editing has attracted increasing attention from the research community. This setting can be broadly categorized into two types: 1) step-wise editing [34, 63, 65, 74], where each editing step is performed independently based on the previous output image and the current instruction; and 2) context-aware editing [12, 44, 64, 67], where the model generates the target image by jointly considering previous text instructions and historically generated images within continuous editing context. Compared with conventional single-turn editing [2, 11, 25, 32, 37, 46, 71], multi-turn image editing better aligns with the iterative workflow of real-world creative scenarios, suggesting substantial potential for practical applications. Realizing this potential requires high-quality training data for both editing scenarios. Sequential rollout with powerful closed-source image editing models is the most common approach to constructing such data, as it combines single-turn edits with scalable generation process [43]. However, this approach reuses each generated image as the input to the next edit, allowing errors and artifacts to accumulate and causing visual-quality drift over longer trajectories. Beyond visual quality, existing datasets are also limited in trajectory length and often cover only one of the two editing scenarios [44, 64, 69]. To address these challenges, we introduce MTEdit, multi-turn image editing dataset constructed through pipeline centered on packed trajectory canvas (PTC) generation. PTC contains multiple panels, each depicting the outcome of one editing turn. Jointly generating these panels within unified visual context reduces visual-quality drift across turns, enabling the construction of high-quality multi-turn trajectories. Specifically, given curated source image, vision-language model (VLM) plans an editing sequence and produces corresponding PTC prompt. The source image and this prompt are then provided to closed-source image editing model (e.g., GPT Image 2 [42] or Nano Banana 2 [20]) to generate the PTC. Gemini 3.1 Pro [21] then filters out failed PTC generations before deriving turn-level editing instructions from each retained PTC and its source image. The retained canvases are subsequently split into target images to form training pairs. Finally, we apply SIFT-based [3] feature matching followed by image warping to improve pixel-level alignment within each editing pair. MTEdit comprises total of 500K multi-turn editing trajectories and 2.69M edit pairs, with 4 to 8 turns per trajectory and an average of 5.38 turns. It covers both step-wise and context-aware editing scenarios and supports 23 common editing categories (see Fig. 3), making it an extensive resource for training multi-turn image editing models. As shown in Tab. 1 and Fig. 1(c), MTEdit offers more trajectories and longer editing sequences than the compared datasets. Formal definitions of step-wise and context-aware editing are provided in Sec. 3.1. Beyond training data, reliable evaluation is essential for understanding model performance across successive editing turns. Although existing benchmarks [8, 44, 61, 65] have begun to assess multi-turn image editing, many use sequences of only around three turns [8, 64, 65, 69], limiting their ability to reveal error accumulation over longer trajectories. Their evaluation protocols also often overlook visual-quality drift across turns. To address these limitations, we introduce MTEdit-Bench for evaluating both step-wise and context-aware editing. It assesses instruction following, content consistency, resistance to visual-quality drift, and the ability to use historical instructions and image states throughout the editing process. To demonstrate the training utility of MTEdit, we fine-tune Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal [39] on the dataset to obtain Qwen-Image-MTEdit. We evaluate broad range of closed-source and open-source image editing models on MTEdit-Bench, including Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Our model achieves the best performance among the evaluated open-source models, demonstrating the effectiveness of MTEdit in improving multi-turn image editing capabilities. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: 1) We introduce MTEdit, comprising 500K multi-turn editing trajectories constructed through PTC generation pipeline that reduces visual-quality drift across turns; 2) We introduce MTEdit-Bench to evaluate both step-wise and context-aware editing in terms of instruction following, content consistency, visual-quality stability, and historical context use; 3) We develop Qwen-Image-MTEdit by fine-tuning on MTEdit, achieving the best performance among the evaluated open-source models on MTEdit-Bench.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Instruction-based Image Editing: Instruction-based image editing (IIE) modifies an input image according to natural language command while preserving instruction-irrelevant visual content. InstructPix2Pix [2] is the first work to formalize this paradigm by leveraging Prompt-to-Prompt [23] to ensure spatial-structure consistency in training data. Recent closed-source models such as the GPT-Image series [4042] and Nano Banana series [1820], together with open-source models such as Step1X-Edit [35], FLUX [31], Qwen-Image-Edit [58], LongCat-Image [50], FireRed-Image-Edit [52], and JoyAI-Image [48], have continued to advance the field. sections.content: largely depends on large-scale, high-quality training data [1, 6, 10, 15, 38, 46, 68, 70]. However, most efforts still focus on single-turn editing, leaving the more interactive multi-turn setting comparatively underexplored. Datasets for Single-turn Image Editing: Most existing image editing datasets are constructed under the single-turn editing setting. Early datasets such as GIER [47] provide human-annotated editing instructions with paired before-andafter images, establishing standard supervision format for instruction-guided image editing. Subsequent datasets scale this paradigm through synthetic or hybrid construction pipelines, including UltraEdit [72], OmniEdit [57], AnyEdit [66], and UniVG [16], while frontier-model-distilled datasets such as Echo-4o-Image [62], HQ-Edit [26], GPT-Image-Edit-1.5M [56] and ShareGPT-4o-Image [7] further expand the scale and complexity of image editing supervision. Despite their effectiveness, these datasets mainly supervise one-step transformations, motivating dedicated datasets that capture coherent editing sequences across multiple successive user interaction turns rather than isolated before-and-after image pairs. Datasets for Multi-turn Image Editing: MagicBrush [69] provides early multi-turn samples for real images, but its trajectories are short, small-scale, and heavily human-annotated. SEED-Data-Edit [17] introduces Photoshopexpert annotations, yet its multi-turn subset remains limited and lacks systematic coverage of context-dependent editing. ImgEdit [64] explores context-aware abilities such as content understanding, content memory, and version backtracking, but it has short editing trajectories and overlooks common step-wise editing data. Pico-Banana400K [43] constructs about 77K multi-turn sequences using Nano Banana, but its rollout pipeline can accumulate errors and introduce visual drift in longer trajectories. VINCIE [44] extracts interleaved image-text sequences from videos for in-context editing, but natural video transitions are insufficient to cover diverse user editing intents. Overall, high-quality, comprehensive, and large-scale datasets for multi-turn image editing remain lacking.

sections.title: 3 Technical Details
sections.content: This section presents the technical details of MTEdit, MTEdit-Bench, and Qwen-Image-MTEdit. Sec. 3.1 first defines the tasks covered by our dataset: step-wise editing and three types of context-aware editing. Sec. 3.2 details the data construction pipeline of MTEdit. Sec. 3.3 analyzes the scale of MTEdit, the distribution of editing types, and its coverage of multi-turn scenarios. Sec. 3.4 introduces the construction of MTEdit-Bench and its automated evaluation protocol. Sec. 3.5 further describes Qwen-Image-MTEdit, which is fine-tuned on MTEdit.

sections.title: 3.1 Task Definition
sections.content: Step-wise Editing is the most common setting in multi-turn image editing and is also the primary form studied in most prior work [34, 65, 74]. In this setting, each editing turn does not explicitly rely on the historical context composed of all previous images and text instructions. Instead, it is mainly conditioned on the image generated in the previous turn and the current user edit prompt. Therefore, models designed for single-turn editing can also be extended to step-wise editing through rollout-style execution. However, for single-turn edit models, this strategy causes errors to accumulate across editing turns. As the number of turns increases, image content, subject consistency, and local details often exhibit noticeable drift [49]. Context-aware Editing requires the model to leverage historical information, rather than relying solely on the latest image and current instruction. We consider three context-aware editing types: (1) persistent-constraint editing, where constraints specified in earlier prompts must remain valid in subsequent turns; (2) textual-reference editing, where later instructions refer to previously introduced or modified objects through pronouns or descriptive phrases; and (3) short-instruction editing, where an initial explicit instruction establishes the edit target and later-turn instructions are brief or underspecified, often requesting adjustments to the degree or intensity of an attribute. 3 Figure 2. Overview of our data construction pipeline. (a) Seed image curation, which selects source images with high resolution and aesthetic quality; (b) PTC generation, in which VLMs derive PTC prompt from each source image to guide closed-source image models in generating the corresponding PTC; and (c) PTC to multi-turn conversion, which processes the generated canvases into multi-turn editing trajectories with turn-level instructions and target images.

sections.title: 3.2 Data Construction Pipeline
sections.content: The data construction pipeline of MTEdit consists of three steps: (a) seed image curation, (b) PTC generation, and (c) PTC to multi-turn conversion, as illustrated in Fig. 2. Seed Image Curation: To construct multi-turn editing trajectories, we first curate seed images that serve as the source images of the trajectories. We collect candidate images from large-scale, openly available image sources [9], including LAION [45], Open Images [28] and DenseFusion [33]. Each retained seed image is used as the initial state of one multi-turn editing trajectory. To ensure that the source images have high visual quality, we apply two filtering criteria: (i) high resolution, requiring the shorter side of the image to be at least 1024 pixels; and (ii) high aesthetic quality, requiring an aesthetic score of at least 8 on 010 scale, as assessed by Gemini 3.1 Pro [21]. The system prompt is in Appendix A.8.1. PTC Generation: common strategy [43] for constructing multi-turn image editing trajectories is to leverage the capabilities of closed-source image editing models and generate data in sequential rollout manner, where the output of each editing turn is used as the input to the next turn. However, the major limitation of this strategy is that visual quality drift becomes increasingly severe as the number of editing turns grows (e.g., beyond four turns). To address this issue, we use closed-source models to generate multiple editing states within single PTC in one pass. By jointly generating targets for multiple editing turns in shared context, this approach reduces visual quality drift and enables longer editing trajectories with better visual quality. Qualitative and quantitative comparisons with rollout-style pipelines are presented in Fig. 8 and Tab. 4 in the appendix, respectively. PTC generation proceeds in two steps. First, we use VLMs to synthesize an instruction for closed-source models from the source image, named PTC prompt. Second, we feed the source image and PTC prompt to closed-source models to obtain the PTC. The generated PTCs are 4K square canvases with four panels in 22 layout, ensuring that each panel retains resolution of approximately 2K, which is sufficient for producing high-quality training data. PTC to Multi-Turn Conversion: After obtaining the PTC, we convert it into multi-turn image editing trajectories. This conversion consists of four steps. First, we use Gemini 3.1 Pro to filter out failed PTC generations, such as those shown in Fig. 13. Second, we feed the source image with the retained PTC into Gemini 3.1 Pro to generate user prompts for each editing turn. Third, we split the PTC into panels according to the 22 layout, and treat each panel as the target image after the corresponding editing turn. Fourth, we apply SIFT-based [3] feature matching 4 Figure 3. Statistics of MTEdit. (a) Edit-type taxonomy, (b) multi-turn data distribution, and (c) instruction word cloud. followed by image warping to improve pixel-level alignment within each editing pair. As result, each sample consists of the source image, turn-level user prompts, and turn-level target images. Moreover, under the default 22 PTC layout, each run of our data construction pipeline produces single four-turn editing sample. To construct longer editing sequences (such as eight-turn samples), we only need to take the generated image from the last turn as the new source image for the next round and rerun the pipeline.

sections.title: 3.3 Dataset Statistics
sections.content: MTEdit contains 500K editing trajectories and 2.69M edit pairs, with up to 8 turns and an average of 5.38 turns per trajectory, and simultaneously covers both step-wise and context-aware multi-turn editing. In terms of the number of turns, the total number of edit pairs, and scenario completeness, our dataset provides broader coverage than the compared multi-turn editing datasets. Fig. 3 further characterizes the distribution of MTEdit from three perspectives. The left subfigure summarizes the edit-type taxonomy used in MTEdit. We organize all edits into two-level hierarchy, with five coarse categories: object structure, object appearance, scene composition, local detail, and atmospheric edits. These coarse categories are further divided into 23 leaf categories. The middle subfigure reports the proportion of each multi-turn data type: step-wise data accounts for 56%, while the remaining 44% are context-aware data, further divided into textual-reference (25%), persistent-constraint (7%) and short-instruction (12%). The right subfigure presents word cloud of all user instructions in MTEdit, illustrating its lexical diversity.

sections.title: 3.4 MTEdit-Bench
sections.content: Benchmark Construction and Task Coverage: MTEdit-Bench comprises source images paired with manually crafted prompts, covering four multi-turn editing tasks: step-wise, persistent-constraint, textual-reference, and short-instruction. The step-wise sub-bench consists of 100 eight-turn samples and mainly evaluates editing performance and visual drift over long editing chains. Each of the three context-aware sub-benches consists of 50 four-turn samples and assesses models use of prior textual prompts and visual states across turns. Evaluation Metrics: MTEdit-Bench uses task-specific metrics to evaluate capabilities required across multi-turn editing scenarios. For the step-wise sub-bench, we report three turn-level metrics: IF (Instruction Following), CC (Content Consistency), and DRS (Drift Robustness Score). IF and CC follow the VLM-judge-based evaluation paradigm used in VIEScore [27], GEdit-Bench [35], Edit-R2 [65], and EdiVal-Agent [8], measuring instruction following and content consistency. To compute IF at each turn, we provide the VLM with the pre-edit image, the models generated image after the edit, and the current-turn instruction. To compute CC, we provide the initial image of the editing sequence, the models generated image at the current turn, and all instructions up to that turn. The VLM assigns each metric score from 0 to 10 (see Appendix A.8 for the system prompts). If either IF or CC falls below 6 at any turn, we consider the editing trajectory to have failed and set both scores to 0 for all subsequent turns. This reflects the causal nature of multi-turn editing: subsequent edits build on an incorrect state after failure and are therefore no longer credited as successful continuation, consistent with the failure-propagation principle used in VINCIE [44]. To balance performance and reproducibility, we use Qwen 3.5 Plus [51] as the VLM evaluator. DRS measures robustness against visual drift and is computed from two drift-sensitive metrics, VisualQuality-R1 [60] and RALI [73]. DRS is calculated as the average of their image quality scores, (VisualQuality-R1 + RALI)/2, and ranges from 0 to 5. This choice is motivated by Banana100 [49], which finds that VisualQuality-R1 and RALI 5 Figure 4. Qualitative results on the step-wise sub-bench. Our method achieves competitive editing performance and maintains visual quality without noticeable degradation across editing turns. reliably detect visual quality degradation during iterative image replication, assigning lower scores to degraded images. We use DRS to evaluate all types of multi-turn editing data. For the remaining three types of context-aware editing, it is necessary to consider whether models can correctly use the historical context. We therefore provide the VLM judge with the full multi-turn editing trajectory, including the instructions and corresponding generated images, allowing it to assess each case within the shared interaction context. We denote the resulting instruction-following and content-consistency scores as IF and CC, respectively. The same failure-propagation rule applies to these two scores; DRS is never zeroed after failure.

sections.title: 4.2 Experimental Results
sections.content: In this subsection, we mainly present and analyze the quantitative and qualitative results of different methods on the step-wise sub-bench. Detailed analyses of the persistent-constraint, textual-reference, and short-instruction sub-benches are provided in the Appendix A.3. Quantitative Results: Tab. 2 presents quantitative comparisons on the step-wise sub-bench. Qwen-Image-MTEdit demonstrates strong resistance to visual drift over long editing sequences: it achieves DRS of 4.33 at Turn 4 and maintains the highest DRS among compared methods through Turn 8. Although it trails the strongest closed-source models in instruction following and content preservation, it achieves state-of-the-art performance among the compared open-source methods. Compared with our base model, Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal [39], Qwen-ImageMTEdit consistently improves IF, CC, and DRS across all eight turns. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of high-quality training data in improving step-wise multi-turn editing performance. Qualitative Results: Fig. 4 presents qualitative comparisons of different models at Turns 4 and 8 of the eight-turn step-wise editing task. The compared methods exhibit two main failure modes. First, methods such as OmniGen2, the FLUX series, SenseNova-U1, and VINCIE struggle to preserve content consistency, producing outputs at Turn 8 that differ substantially from the source image beyond the intended edits. Second, most methods, including closed-source models, exhibit increasing visual quality drift as editing progresses. For example, noticeable artifacts appear in the sky at Turn 8. In comparison, our model better preserves visual quality across editing turns and produces no obvious artifacts in the final turn.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation Studies
sections.content: To isolate the effect of PTC generation on editing performance, we conduct controlled ablation comparing it with sequential rollout under matched data and training budgets. Using Nano Banana 2 [20], each approach produces 10,000 eight-turn step-wise trajectories from identical source images and per-turn edit prompts. We 8 fine-tune the same Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal [39] base model on each dataset for 5,000 steps with identical training hyperparameters, then evaluate both models on the eight-turn step-wise sub-bench of MTEdit-Bench. As shown in Tab. 3, training on data constructed via PTC generation yields higher IF from Turn 2 onward and higher CC at every turn than training on sequential rollout data. It also improves resistance to visual drift: the model trained on PTC-generated data achieves higher DRS from Turn 3 onward and maintains scores between 4.17 and 4.26 across all eight turns. At Turn 8, its DRS is 4.22, compared with 3.96 for the model trained on sequential rollout data. Fig. 5 compares visual quality at Turn 8. The model trained on sequential rollout data exhibits pronounced texture artifacts on the cats face and fur, whereas the model trained on PTC-generated data preserves cleaner fur, whiskers, and bell details, as highlighted in enlarged crops. These results show that the reduced visual quality drift of PTC-generated training data translates into better instruction following, content consistency, and visual quality stability in multi-turn editing.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: In this work, we present MTEdit, large-scale dataset for multi-turn image editing. MTEdit provides training data covering both step-wise and context-aware editing, constructed through PTC generation pipeline that reduces visual quality drift across turns. We also introduce MTEdit-Bench, which evaluates instruction following, content consistency, visual-quality stability, and the ability to use historical context. Fine-tuning Qwen-Image-Edit-Causal on our dataset yields Qwen-Image-MTEdit, which demonstrates strong performance on long-chain step-wise editing and competitive context-aware editing capabilities, highlighting the value of high-quality multi-turn supervision. We hope that MTEdit will support further research toward more reliable and context-aware multi-turn image editing in real-world creative workflows and increasingly complex downstream applications.

A.1 Qwen-Image-MTEdit Details Qwen-Image-MTEdit is obtained by supervised fine-tuning the single-turn editing model Qwen-Image-EditCausal [39] on MTEdit. To adapt the model to multi-turn editing, we make two structural modifications. First, we use block causal attention [53], which allows the current editing turn to attend to image states and text instructions from previous turns while preventing access to future turns. This causal structure avoids information leakage during training, supports parallel computation of turn-level objectives within single forward pass, and enables KV-Cache [24, 54] reuse over historical contexts at inference time. Second, we replace the original 3D RoPE with 3D interleaved RoPE [22, 55]. Image and text tokens are organized into an interleaved sequence following the temporal order of multi-turn editing, i.e., [Image] - [Text] - [Image] - .... Each image-text unit corresponds to the image state and editing instruction of one editing turn. This positional encoding helps the model distinguish images and instructions from different turns, aligns each instruction with its corresponding editing state, and supports longer editing sequences [22]. During training, we use AdamW [36] with fixed learning rate of 5105, weight decay of 102, and (𝛽1, 𝛽2) = (0.9, 0.999). We train Qwen-Image-MTEdit for 20,000 steps on 32 H100 GPUs with per-GPU batch size of 1 using bfloat16 mixed precision.
